newsitem.title: HAITI: Death threats, cash crunch as Haiti schools open.
newsitem.headline: Death threats, cash crunch as Haiti schools open.

text.p: Haiti's schoolchildren headed back to class on Monday facing death threats from angry soldiers and severe shortages of basic school supplies as the beleaguered education system struggled to get back on its feet.

"This is the most difficult year," said Education Minister Jacques Edouard Alexis, visibly stressed by the task of getting more than one million children into classrooms. "I've been here since March and I still can't find the money to provide the minimum for the schools."

The problems of Haiti's schools are just one of the hurdles facing residents of the impoverished Caribbean nation as it fights to restore basic services after more than a year of political turmoil and fiscal crisis.

Children heading to class on Monday in neat uniforms and bright hair ribbons were targets of threatened violence by former soldiers who have repeatedly warned parents not to send children to school if their demands for back pay are not met.

Former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide disbanded Haiti's military when he was restored to power in 1994 and some ex-soldiers have said schoolchildren will suffer unless they get pay and pensions they say they are owed.

Radio stations have broadcast menacing news releases from the ex-soldiers and a cassette tape reiterating the threats was found last week among "subversive" paraphernalia at the home of Emmanuel "Toto" Constant, leader of a feared paramilitary group that allegedly carried out much of the repression during the coup years, authorities said.

"The tape was presumably meant for distrubution to radio stations," Haitian National Police Chief Pierre Denize said. "The ex-military is playing a card here, a very dangerous card. Not only will it turn people against them, but all it would take is for a few of them to shoot some automatic weapons near a school and there would be a general panic."

Parents acknowledged that the ex-soldiers are dangerous but many refused to be cowed by their threats. "What kind of a person threatens to hurt a child as means to get money?" asked one mother as she ironed uniforms on her front porch.

Other parents expressed disappointment that politics could once again disrupt the school year. "Last year was the first time in ten years there was a full school year," said another mother. "It was considered a great success for democracy."

Even if the soldiers' threats prove hollow, Haiti's schools face daunting financial problems. Many of the children arriving in class on Monday will find no toilets, water, desks or trained teachers due to a severe federal budget deficit.
International aid was expected to close a budget gap of more than $100 million but only if Haiti moves forward with its difficult plan to privatise government-owned businesses.
"Last year, there was lots of international aid, negotiated by Aristide," said Alexis, the education minister. "But this year, everything was put together and conditioned on a privatisation law."

The budget crunch has been felt acutely by families in Haiti, where officials say 60 percent of the people earn less than $100 per year. Unemployment has risen to 80 percent, according to The Washington Office on Haiti.
"I never go to school," said a nine-year-old boy named Jean begging in front of the National Palace. "My family doesn't even have enough money to eat, and I'm very hungry."
